findings.title: Findings converge on the cross-tree pairing mechanism (matching kinds, predicate, and tie-break order)
findings.why_it_matters: Four findings from both critics land on one mechanism: how a head finding is paired with a base finding. D5 pairs on equality, D6 pairs on containment, D10 adds a catalog field to route between the kinds, and both D5 and D6 use a rename-mapped "same file first, then any file" tie-break. The Senior Engineer shows the tie-break order is unspecified and can blame an untouched file (Finding 4). The Minimalist argues that equality and containment are one algorithm with two predicates (Finding 6), that the catalog field then has one consumer (Finding 7), and that the run-wide rename map exists only to break ties (Finding 8). Each proposes its own patch: a two-pass order, a merged predicate, a deleted field, a scoped rename map. Is the pairing mechanism itself under-specified, so it should be re-evaluated as a whole (how many matching kinds, what predicate, what deterministic pairing order, whether path preference uses the rename map at all, whether the routing needs a catalog field), rather than patched four times?
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate the pairing mechanism before addressing the converging findings individually.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate the pairing mechanism before addressing the converging findings individually. Open questions: how many matching kinds are needed; whether the predicate is equality, containment, or equality first and then containment; what deterministic order pairs findings (per-finding greedy, per-pass, or maximum matching); whether same-file preference needs the rename map; and whether routing needs a catalog field or a branch.
findings.choice_reason: Settled: pass-based pairing, exact before containment, run-wide rename map and base_match kept

findings.title: Findings converge on HSL102's line-count source (D7 reading the extractions outside the scan)
findings.why_it_matters: D7 counts head and base lines by reading files from the extractions after the scans, using the rename map to find the base path and counting 0 when the path is missing. Three findings from both critics land on this one mechanism. It is a second read outside `load_file` on a path discovery never vetted (Finding 9). Its "count 0" infers the base state, which can disagree with what the base scan saw: a file excluded, decode-failed, or pragma-suppressed at base (Finding 10). And the base scan already knows whether the base file was over the threshold (Finding 7). Both critics independently propose taking the base side from the base scan instead. Should D7's line-count source be re-evaluated (whether extraction reads are needed at all, what an unreadable or excluded base file means, whether HSL102 needs a catalog hook) before patching each finding?
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate HSL102's line-count source before addressing the converging findings individually.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate HSL102's line-count source before addressing the converging findings individually. Open questions: whether reading the extractions is needed at all; what an unreadable, excluded, or suppressed base file means for the ratchet; whether HSL102 needs a catalog hook.
findings.choice_reason: Settled: base scan decides; counts round-trip through file_length.py's own message

findings.title: The design never says the head config comes from the HEAD extraction, or how it is resolved there
findings.why_it_matters: D4 says "the head tree's config" and step 2 says "the working tree is never read". Today the only path is `cli.check` → `resolve_project(root, config)` from the cwd → `load_config`, which reads the working tree. Run unchanged, an uncommitted `max_lines` or `select` edit changes the gate for the committed code. That is flaw 2 again, this time for config. The design maps the root (line 30) and an explicit `--config` (line 112) into each extraction, but doesn't say how the config is found inside the extraction or what happens when the HEAD commit has no config at that path (for example, a config file that exists only uncommitted). If resolution inside the extraction ever runs without an explicit root, `resolve_project` walks up past the extraction (discovery.py:547-556). It stops only at a `.git` entry, which an extraction lacks, so a stray `/tmp/pyproject.toml` could apply. Line 30 implies an explicit root, which avoids that walk, but the design doesn't say so.
findings.chosen: A: Say in D4 that `new_code` resolves the root and config in the working tree only to get their repo-relative paths, then loads the config from the same path in the HEAD extraction with an explicit root (no upward discovery). With no config at that path in HEAD, the run uses the default config, as a normal run with no config does.
findings.recommended: A: Say in D4 that `new_code` resolves the root and config in the working tree only to get their repo-relative paths, then loads the config from the same path in the HEAD extraction with an explicit root (no upward discovery). With no config at that path in HEAD, the run uses the default config, as a normal run with no config does.

findings.title: D6's containment pairing order is unspecified and greedy, so the finding reported as new can land on an old, untouched occurrence
findings.why_it_matters: Containment is symmetric and not transitive, so one short occurrence can pair with many base occurrences. D5's wording (line 137) is per head finding: try the same file, then any file. D6's wording ("same file first, then any file, one to one") is ambiguous between that and two passes. Under the per-finding reading, take a base with copies A and B (200 lines each) and a PR that adds a short copy X in file C whose text is inside A. If X is visited first, it takes base-A through the any-file fallback. Head-A then falls back to base-B, and head-B is left over and reported as new. The count is right, but the CI annotation points at untouched file B and X goes unreported. Running the same-file pass over all findings before the any-file pass avoids this case. The design doesn't say which it does.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1
findings.recommended: A: Specify pass-based pairing in D5 and D6: equality first (same file, then any file), then containment for the rest, with ties broken by smallest length difference and then path. Add a test for the long-plus-short case.

findings.title: `git diff -M` warnings on large PRs fail the gate through `run_git`'s "any stderr is failure" rule
findings.why_it_matters: `run_git` raises `GitFailure` on any non-empty stderr, even with exit 0 (discovery.py:158-173). When rename candidates exceed `diff.renameLimit`, git prints `warning: exhaustive rename detection was skipped due to too many files` to stderr. Reusing `run_git`, the natural reuse, turns a large move or split PR into a hard error, and that is the PR HSL102 pushes people to make. The rename output also depends on user config (`diff.renames`, `diff.renameLimit`, `core.quotepath`) unless the flags are pinned, and without `-z` git quotes non-ASCII names. A rename below git's 50% similarity default gets base count 0, so it is reported as new growth, and the design doesn't say whether that's accepted.
findings.chosen: A: Specify `git diff -z --name-status -M -l0` through `run_git` in D7. State that a rename below the similarity threshold counts as a new file (base 0).
findings.recommended: A: Specify `git diff -z --name-status -M -l0` through `run_git` in D7. State that a rename below the similarity threshold counts as a new file (base 0).

findings.title: HSL104 containment could fold into the generic matcher, leaving HSL102 the only special case
findings.why_it_matters: D5 (equality on whitespace-free span text) and D6 (containment on the same text) are the same pairing over the same inputs with a different predicate. A single matcher using "equal or one contains the other" would need no HSL104 hook. The real difference is the message: HSL104's message counts places (`duplicated code of N lines in K places`, duplicate_code.py:161), so it changes whenever a copy is added, and the key would have to drop or normalise the message for HSL104. The cost is a looser D5. Containment for every rule passes edits that extend a flagged span (`X=1` → `X=10` for HSL004), and lets a short new finding match a longer old one elsewhere, for example a new `# TODO` comment inside an old `# TODO: fix later`. That reverses D5's ratified "touching it re-reports it" row.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1
findings.recommended: B: Keep separate equality and containment kinds, as ratified.

findings.title: HSL102 may not need a catalog hook or extraction counting; the base scan's own HSL102 finding answers most cases
findings.why_it_matters: Under D4 both runs use the head config, so if the base scan has no HSL102 finding at the mapped path, the base file was at or under the threshold, the head is over it, and the finding is new. Only when both have a finding is a count comparison needed. That removes the "count 0 for a new file" special case and most of the extraction reads. If Finding 6 is also applied, `base_match` (D10) has one consumer and could be a branch. The catch: when both findings exist, the base count has to come from somewhere, either the message (which D7's deciding factor rejects) or a read.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1
findings.recommended: A: Derive "new" from the base scan's HSL102 finding, and read line counts only when both trees have one.

findings.title: The rename map is run-wide machinery that only D7 strictly needs
findings.why_it_matters: Step 1 computes the rename map for every run, and D5 and D6 use it only to prefer the same file when several identically keyed findings tie. For D5's equality key, the count of new findings per key is max(0, head − base) whatever the pairing, so the map changes only which finding is cited. D7 can't work without it. Dropping it from D5 and D6 makes the matcher take only findings and text, with no path translation. The counterpoint is Finding 4: which finding is cited is what CI annotations show, and for D6's containment, pairing order can matter beyond the citation.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: D7 reads files a second time outside `load_file`, on a base path discovery never vetted
findings.why_it_matters: CLAUDE.md requires each scanned file to be read once through `source.load_file`, and discovery's containment check vets symlinks. D7 reads head and base files "directly" to count lines. A base path from the rename map never went through discovery, so a tracked symlink at base pointing outside the extraction would be followed. The count must also match the detector's decoding (BOM, encoding cookie), and a separate read risks a second decoding implementation that drifts. The cache-coherence reason behind the CLAUDE.md rule matters less here, since the extraction is private and nothing edits it mid-run. The symlink and decoding concerns remain.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 2
findings.recommended: A: Say in D7 that counts come from the scans, or from `load_file` and `parse_python` on a contained path, never a raw read.

findings.title: HSL102's base state is inferred from the extraction and can disagree with the base scan
findings.why_it_matters: "Count 0 when the file didn't exist at base" is inferred from the rename map and the base extraction. If the base file exists but failed to decode or parse, was excluded, or carried `ignore-file HSL102`, the extraction path and the base scan disagree, and D7 doesn't say which wins. `file_length.detect` uses `source.text`, which exists only for a parsed file, so a base file that didn't decode has no count from the detector's path. Counting it as 0 makes every head HSL102 finding for it look like growth.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 2
findings.recommended: A: State in D7 that a base file without a count counts as 0, so its head HSL102 finding is new. It matches "a file added with too many lines counts as growing from 0".

findings.title: The cache location type may be a bigger refactor than splitting the flag needs
findings.why_it_matters: The need is to scan an extraction while using the real root's default cache, with the managed-default treatment (self-ignore marker and symlink check). Today `run_scan` derives both from `cache_dir is None` (pipeline.py:204, 227), and `prepare_cache_dir` already takes `self_ignore` as a keyword (cache.py:442). The design replaces `cache_dir: Path | None` with a location type through `RunCache` and `cache.py`. The Minimalist suggests two explicit keyword parameters on `run_scan` (`cache_base`, plus a caller-decided managed flag) instead. The critic overstates one point: a one-parameter fix isn't enough, because passing the default path as an explicit `cache_dir` loses the symlink check. Two values are needed either way, so the choice is between a small type and two parameters.
findings.chosen: B: Keep the location type, but stop it at `run_scan` and `RunCache`. `cache.py`'s functions keep their explicit `self_ignore` bool.
findings.recommended: B: Keep the location type, but stop it at `run_scan` and `RunCache`. `cache.py`'s functions keep their explicit `self_ignore` bool.

findings.title: D5's "swap" row overstates what it catches: a swap with identical text passes
findings.why_it_matters: The D5 table says that fixing one lazy import and adding a different one in the same file is reported as New. The key is rule, message, and whitespace-free span text, with no path. So when the removed and added findings have the same text (HSL002 `import json` in `f()` fixed, `import json` added in `g()`, or in another file), they match and the swap passes. The debt moves. That follows from the ratified "moves pass" stance, but the table row reads as though swaps are always caught.
findings.chosen: A: Reword the D5 swap row to separate different-text swaps (New) from identical-text swaps (pass).
findings.recommended: A: Reword the D5 swap row to separate different-text swaps (New) from identical-text swaps (pass).

findings.title: Skip the base extraction and scan when the head run has no findings
findings.why_it_matters: With zero head findings there's nothing to subtract, so the merge-base lookup, the base extraction, and the base scan can all be skipped. That halves the cost of a clean run, house-lint linting itself for example. It does nothing for a backlog repo like hassette. It also changes behaviour slightly: a base-only scan error, which Posture says fails the run, would no longer be seen.
findings.chosen: B: Always run both scans.
findings.recommended: B: Always run both scans.

findings.title: A base-only scan error fails the PR that fixes it
findings.why_it_matters: Posture says an error from either run fails the gate. A parse or decode failure, or a jscpd failure, that exists only at the merge-base therefore fails a PR whose purpose is to fix it. Parse failures are error results (scanner.py:57, 91). This is raised once, against a ratified posture.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a scan error present only at the merge-base fails the gate, so the PR fixing it has to merge without the gate.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a scan error present only at the merge-base fails the gate, so the PR fixing it has to merge without the gate.

findings.title: Extraction depends on git environment and checkout state the design doesn't pin
findings.why_it_matters: `run_git` inherits the environment on purpose (discovery.py:158-162). Inside hooks, `GIT_DIR`, `GIT_INDEX_FILE` or `GIT_WORK_TREE` may be set, and the design overrides only `GIT_INDEX_FILE` for `read-tree`. The critic also raises sparse checkouts (skip-worktree bits making `checkout-index` skip files) and blobless clones (blob fetches mid-run). Nothing checks that an extraction is complete, so a silent partial extraction would make findings vanish from both trees, against Posture's "fail loudly". The sparse-checkout mechanism is unverified: a fresh temporary index from a plain `read-tree` may not carry skip-worktree bits at all.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: extraction assumes a full, non-sparse clone and an ordinary hook environment.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: extraction assumes a full, non-sparse clone and an ordinary hook environment.

findings.title: Temporary extractions leak on SIGKILL or timeout and copy every tracked file
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: larger repos than hassette. "Always removed" holds for exceptions, not for SIGKILL, a CI timeout, or an interrupted hook. Each leaked directory is a full copy of every tracked file, binary assets included, though only configured languages are scanned.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a killed run can leave its temporary extractions in the system temp directory.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a killed run can leave its temporary extractions in the system temp directory.

findings.title: The `--base` ref is passed to git without verification
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: CI where the ref name isn't controlled by the maintainer. The design never says the ref is protected from being read as an option, so a value starting with `-` would be. Git refnames can't start with `-`, so `github.base_ref` can't trigger it. The input is the user's own CLI argument.
findings.chosen: A: Resolve the ref with `rev-parse --verify --end-of-options <ref>^{commit}` before any other git call, and use the SHA from then on.
findings.recommended: A: Resolve the ref with `rev-parse --verify --end-of-options <ref>^{commit}` before any other git call, and use the SHA from then on.

findings.title: Findings converge on the pairing-evidence path (the line map, the matcher inputs, and Tree's read cache)
findings.why_it_matters: Three findings from two critics land on one mechanism: how the gate gathers per-file evidence (span text, renames, and the build-time difflib line map) and hands it to every rule's matcher. Finding 2 says the line map was added at build time without ratification and only changes which finding gets blamed. Finding 3 says the matcher signature grew to six keyword inputs, repeated in five places, and the line map was the latest addition. Finding 4 says `Tree` carries a mutable read cache inside a frozen dataclass, which exists so span text and the line map share one read per file. The structural-minimalist traces the last two directly to the line map: "Both come from the line-map addition rather than from the ratified design." Patching each one separately (bundle the inputs, swap the cache for a dict, ratify the map) settles three coupled questions in isolation. Does this point to a design problem in the evidence path that should be re-evaluated as a whole, or are these three independent tidy-ups? Re-evaluation includes whether the line map is needed at all, and whether wrong blame for identical findings is a limitation to accept and document.
findings.recommended: A: Re-evaluate the pairing-evidence path before addressing Findings 2, 3, and 4 individually. Open questions: Is blaming the right one of several identical findings worth a per-file diff on every run? Which inputs does each matcher actually need, and should a new input cost a signature change? Which component owns reading an extracted file, and does more than one consumer need that read?
findings.chosen: A: Re-evaluate the pairing-evidence path before addressing Findings 2, 3, and 4 individually.
findings.choice_reason: Dropped the line map (no peer tracks which identical occurrence is new); kept keyword matcher inputs

findings.title: The difflib line map is unratified, changes only which finding is blamed, and is tested only below difflib's 200-line autojunk threshold
findings.why_it_matters: The count of new findings per key is `max(0, head - base)` whatever the pairing order, so the line map never changes whether the gate passes. It only picks which of several identical findings is reported. Without it, a finding inserted above identical old ones blamed the last old occurrence (design.md:294). That build call was never ratified, even though the sketch challenge had questioned blame-only machinery. It costs a second read-back and a `SequenceMatcher` per head file that has a located finding. It is also why `Tree` grew a cache (Finding 4) and the matcher signature grew a sixth input (Finding 3). Both tests that pin it use small files, so the autojunk heuristic, which applies only to sequences of 200+ lines and which the code comment keeps on to avoid quadratic time (new_code.py:340-342), is never exercised. When the map misaligns, pairing falls back to first-fit, so the gate blames the wrong occurrence again. The structural-minimalist's cheaper alternative (a), first-fit from the end of the file, only flips which case is wrong: it gets an insert at the top right and an append at the bottom wrong.
findings.recommended: A: Keep the map, ratify it as a D5 addendum ("blame accuracy among identical findings"), and add a 200+ line test whose flagged line repeats.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: Every matcher takes six keyword inputs, repeated in five signatures, and most matchers ignore most of them
findings.why_it_matters: `BaseMatcher` takes `head`, `base`, `head_text`, `base_text`, `renames`, and `line_map`. HSL102's `match_new` uses only `renames` and accepts the other three to satisfy the protocol. The same four-keyword block is spelled out in `exact_passes`, `match_by_key`, both rule matchers, and `new_findings`. Adding `line_map` at build time edited all of them. D10 ratified "one field on the row" so a rule's matching lives in its own module, and this signature churn works against that goal.
findings.recommended: A: Bundle `head_text`, `base_text`, `renames`, and `line_map` into one frozen dataclass (`Evidence` or `Comparison`) passed as a single argument. `BaseMatcher` becomes a `Callable` alias and the Protocol class goes away.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: `Tree` is a frozen dataclass that mutates a hidden read cache and rewrites error messages by string replacement
findings.why_it_matters: `Tree` holds the extraction directory and mapped root. It also holds a mutable `read_back` dict, marked `compare=False` inside a `frozen=True` dataclass, and an `in_project()` method that repairs messages by replacing the temp path string. A reader has to learn that a frozen object mutates. The cache exists only so `span_texts` and `line_map` share one read per file, and both are called in the same place in `run_gate`. `in_project` infers a message's origin from whether it contains the literal temp path. It holds because the workspace is `.resolve()`d before use, as the contract-caller confirmed, but a tool reporting the path in another spelling (relative, or quoted differently, such as jscpd's) would leak the temp path. The critic's proposal to do the replace "at the one place errors are labelled" misses that `in_project` has two callers: `labelled` and `load_head_config`'s `ConfigError` path.
findings.recommended: B: Build a plain `dict[str, list[str] | None]` per tree in `run_gate` before `span_texts` and `line_map`, pass it to both, and reduce `Tree` to its two paths plus `in_project`.
findings.chosen: Superseded by Finding 1

findings.title: `--select <rule> --base` makes HSL900 fail a per-rule gate on any newly added pragma
findings.why_it_matters: The ledger's stated payoff is that hassette and hass-hassette delete their scripts (design.md:12), and the PR-label override stays a thin per-repo wrapper (design.md:22). hassette runs two gates with two label overrides, and each old script judged only its own rule. The gate's exit code covers every finding, so the obvious per-rule invocation is `--select HSL102 --base`. Narrowing selection makes always-on HSL900 flag every pragma for an unselected rule as "unused suppression for disabled rule" (suppressions.py:197-199). hassette's workflow already avoids `--select` for exactly this reason (hassette lint.yml:383-392). Under `--base`, old pragmas pair as old, so only a PR that adds a pragma fails, which makes the failure intermittent and confusing. The file-size gate fails on an unrelated pragma, and the wrong label's override applies. Neither the README nor the ledger says how a per-rule gate should be built. Peers differ here: the prior-art brief (row 5b) records that Ruff's and Pylint's unused-suppression checks are selectable and non-failing. A probe confirms that Ruff's RUF100 reports "non-enabled" codes only when RUF100 itself is selected, so `ruff check --select E501` alone stays clean.
findings.recommended: B: Add a README sentence that a per-rule gate runs the configured rule set and filters the JSON on `rule_id`, explaining why `--select` doesn't work, and carry the same guidance into the hassette and hass-hassette follow-up issues.
findings.chosen: A: Under CLI `--select`, HSL900 doesn't report pragmas naming unselected rules. Ship as its own issue and PR, since it changes HSL900 outside the gate.
findings.choice_reason: Filed as #91; next release waits for it

findings.title: Several ratified gate behaviors have no test pinning them
findings.why_it_matters: The ledger decides that `--fail-on-empty` judges the head scan (design.md:31), but no test mentions it and neither the README nor docs/configuration.md says what it does under `--base`. D5's comb ratified span text decoded through the language layer (encoding cookie, BOM, unreadable file keys on message alone, design.md:152), but nothing exercises `file_lines`, `span_of`, or `span_texts`. The only unreadable-file test works at matcher level. Also unpinned: `--select`/`--ignore` reaching both runs through `SelectionOverrides`, which is the invocation hassette will use; HSL900 being "matched like any other rule" (design.md:154), which is Finding 5's trigger; and a `head run:` error, since only the base side is tested. A later change to any of these passes the suite silently.
findings.chosen: Add integration tests to tests/integration/test_base_gate.py: (1) `--fail-on-empty --base` with no files at HEAD and a non-empty base exits 1, and a non-empty head with an empty base exits 0; (2) a `# -*- coding: latin-1 -*-` file and a BOM file whose old findings pair as old across commits; (3) `--select` and `--ignore` applied to both scans; (4) an unchanged HSL900 pragma finding stays old while a newly added one is new; (5) a parse error only at HEAD is reported with the `head run:` prefix. Add one README sentence to the New-code gating bullets: under `--base`, `--fail-on-empty` judges the head commit's scan. Leave non-ASCII column slicing unpinned until Finding 7 is decided.

findings.title: Span text slices character columns as UTF-8 bytes, so a tokenizer-based finding's key is truncated on non-ASCII lines
findings.why_it_matters: `Finding.column` and `end_column` mean UTF-8 bytes for AST and jscpd findings but characters for line and token findings. `candidate_for_line` ends at `len(line) + 1` in characters (analysis.py:113-115), used by HSL001 and others, and HSL900's `_diagnostic` uses tokenizer columns (suppressions.py:409-417). `span_of` slices encoded bytes at `end_column - 1` (new_code.py:381-388). On a line with a non-ASCII character, such as an em dash in a comment, the key loses its last bytes and can split a character. The build note says the shift is "identical at both commits" (design.md:289), but that's only true when the tails are equal. Two lines with the same message whose text differs only in the truncated tail get equal keys, so a new finding pairs as old and silently passes the gate. The collision itself is rare. The shape costs something on every read: one field with two units, and a consumer that assumes one.
findings.recommended: C: Document the truncation in `span_of`'s docstring and correct the build note now, and file an issue to unify `Finding`'s column unit across rules.
findings.chosen: A: Make line and token findings report UTF-8 byte columns, as AST and jscpd findings do, so `span_of` is right for every rule.

findings.title: An explicit `--config` missing from HEAD silently runs under the built-in config
findings.why_it_matters: D4 ratified defaulting to the built-in config when HEAD has none at the config's path, "accepting that an uncommitted new config is silently ignored" (design.md:124), and the build applied it literally to an explicit `--config` (design.md:287). The comb's later ratification for an out-of-repo `--config` rests on a different principle: "the gate never runs under a config the user didn't ask for" (design.md:126). A user who types `--config new.toml` without committing it gets the built-in config, exit 0, and no note. The only trace is `config: null` in the JSON. Posture says fail loudly. A test pins the current behavior on purpose.
findings.recommended: B: Raise a usage error when an explicit `--config` has no file at its path in HEAD, and leave the discovered-config default as ratified.
findings.chosen: B: Raise a usage error when an explicit `--config` has no file at its path in HEAD, and leave the discovered-config default as ratified.

findings.title: README promises fast repeated runs, but HSL104, which the README's own example turns on, runs jscpd on both commits every time
findings.why_it_matters: The README bullet says both scans share the project's cache "so a repeated run is fast". Project-phase results are never cached (CLAUDE.md Gotchas; docs/rules.md HSL104 "Every run"), so under `--base` jscpd runs twice on every invocation, and D3 always scans both commits even when the head is clean. The README's CI example passes `--extend-select HSL102,HSL104`. D8's speed evidence (7.2s cold, 0.9s warm on hassette) covers only the file phase. hassette's old duplicate gate ran its second scan only when the head found something (lint.yml:453-455), so this is also a cost change from the scripts being replaced. Neither critic asks to reverse D3, only to stop overpromising.
findings.chosen: Reword the README bullet to: "Both scans share the project's cache, so file rules are fast on a repeated run. `HSL104` isn't cached, so jscpd runs on both commits every time."

findings.title: A ref that names no commit, the usual shallow-checkout failure, drops the fetch-history hint
findings.why_it_matters: `run_git` gained a `hint` so `--base` failures end with fetch advice (design.md build calls). `resolve_commits` catches the `GitFailure` for an unresolvable ref and raises `GateFailure(f"--base {ref!r} does not name a commit")` with no hint. `from exc` discards the hint text from the user-facing message. A checkout without `fetch-depth: 0`, or one where `origin/<base>` was never fetched, produces exactly this error, while the missing-merge-base path does say "fetch full history". The two failures one missing fetch can cause read inconsistently.
findings.chosen: Change the message in `resolve_commits` to `f"--base {ref!r} does not name a commit; {GIT_HINT}"` and update the pinned assertion in `test_a_ref_that_names_no_commit_fails_the_run`.

findings.title: `base_match` is declared on both row subclasses, so `base_matcher()` needs an isinstance check and an HSL900 comment
findings.why_it_matters: D10 ratified a catalog field, and this finding doesn't dispute it. The field is declared identically on `FileRule` and `ProjectRule`, both defaulting to `None`, and `base_matcher()` needs `isinstance(rule, (FileRule, ProjectRule))` plus a comment explaining HSL900's bare `Rule` row. One field lives in two places that must stay in sync. `languages` uses the same isinstance pattern (rule_catalog.py:275), but its type and default differ between the subclasses, so it can't be hoisted. `base_match` is identical on both and can.
findings.chosen: Declare `base_match: BaseMatcher = field(default=match_by_key, kw_only=True)` once on `Rule`, remove it from `FileRule` and `ProjectRule`, default the `configurable_rule`/`configurable_project_rule` parameter to `match_by_key`, and reduce `base_matcher` to `return RULES[rule_id].base_match`. Because the field is `kw_only`, the subclasses' positional constructors are unaffected.

findings.title: The only signal for which scan an error came from is a message prefix
findings.why_it_matters: Errors from both runs share `code`, `phase`, `operation`, and `path`. Only `message` differs (`labelled`, new_code.py:391-400). The README tells consumers to "match on rule IDs, locations, and error `code` values". It says finding messages may change but is silent on error messages, and its `--base` bullet documents the prefix. A wrapper that wanted to let a base-only error through, the case D3 says has to merge without the gate, would have to string-match the message. The build call kept the error schema unchanged, though Posture allows breaking it.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a consumer that tells base errors from head errors matches the documented `base run:`/`head run:` message prefix.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a consumer that tells base errors from head errors matches the documented `base run:`/`head run:` message prefix.

findings.title: A failed gate emits no `base` object, so its JSON looks like an ordinary run's
findings.why_it_matters: `findings` means "new findings only" exactly when `base` is present, and `base` is present only on success. The failure branch builds a `ScanResult` without a comparison. A consumer that keys on `payload["base"]` to confirm delta semantics reads a failed gate as "not in gate mode". The failed result's `config` is the explicit `--config` or null, while a successful gate with a discovered config reports the head config's path. Exit 3 and the `errors` array still mark the failure.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: `base` appears only on a completed comparison, and exit code plus `errors` are authoritative.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: `base` appears only on a completed comparison, and exit code plus `errors` are authoritative.

findings.title: Every gate-level git failure is reported as phase `base`, operation `resolve`
findings.why_it_matters: A failed `read-tree`, `checkout-index`, rename `diff`, an unresolvable ref, and not being in a repository all become `error("git", "base", "resolve", ...)`. A consumer keying on `operation` can't tell a bad ref from a failed extraction. The README's `git-error` row ("git failed inside a repository, or `--base` couldn't resolve its commits") doesn't cover being outside a repository.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: every `--base` setup failure reports operation `resolve`. The exit code and `code` are what consumers use.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: every `--base` setup failure reports operation `resolve`. The exit code and `code` are what consumers use.

findings.title: Under `--base`, `shadowed_config` describes the working tree, not the HEAD config that governed
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: a project with two competing config sources that differ between the working tree and HEAD, which is rare for a solo maintainer. The CLI computes the shadowed list from the working tree before `run_gate` and never updates it, while `config` names the HEAD config. The output can list a shadowed config for a resolution that wasn't used. The build call recorded this as informational.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: under `--base`, the shadowed-config note reflects the working tree's config sources.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: under `--base`, the shadowed-config note reflects the working tree's config sources.

findings.title: A filesystem failure during extraction surfaces as a generic internal error
findings.why_it_matters: Audience assumption: CI or hook runs where nobody is at the terminal. `run_gate` catches only `GitFailure` and `GateFailure`. An `OSError` from `tempfile`, `mkdir`, or writing two copies of every tracked file (a full `/tmp`) falls through to the CLI's blanket `except Exception`. That reports an internal error with exit 4, and the traceback appears only under `--debug`. `--debug` also passes through to both scans, so cache diagnostics appear twice with no head or base label.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: a filesystem failure while extracting reports a generic internal error (exit 4), with details under `--debug`.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: a filesystem failure while extracting reports a generic internal error (exit 4), with details under `--debug`.

findings.title: HSL102 recovers line counts by parsing its own message and reads "no base finding" as under-threshold
findings.why_it_matters: `line_count_of` parses `"N lines (threshold: M)"` back out of the message. D7 ratified this round-trip and a test covers it. Separately, "no base finding at this path" is read as "under threshold, unreadable, excluded, or suppressed at base", and all of these count as new, as the docstring says. If `format_message` changes without the regex, a `ValueError` is raised mid-gate. Both live in one module today. The critic recommends no change.
findings.recommended: B: Accept as a known limitation: HSL102's message format and its parser must change together, and any absence at base counts as growth.
findings.chosen: B: Accept as a known limitation: HSL102's message format and its parser must change together, and any absence at base counts as growth.
